newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl and Waigel press for tight EU stability pact.
newsitem.headline: Kohl and Waigel press for tight EU stability pact.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl voiced confidence on Thursday that the European Union would agree on a stability pact for its euro currency, but Finance Minister Theo Waigel hinted he still would not budge on its strict terms.

Kohl told parliament one day before the EU summit in Dublin that he was sure the 15-nation bloc would find a way to launch its economic and monetary union (EMU) on time in 1999, with firm guarantees the euro would enjoy long-term stability.
He also told Germany's critics abroad that Bonn did not seek hegemony in Europe but wanted a flexible approach to allow more integration wherever possible.

Waigel, father of the "stability pact" due to dominate the two-day Dublin meeting, made clear he still wanted clear penalities for EMU members who overstep budget deficit limits and "verifiable definitions" for any exceptions to this rule.

Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens backed EMU but accused Bonn of pushing such a strict line on safeguards that it risked boosting unemployment in Europe and undermining the pro-European majority in neighbouring France.

Germany has come in for heavy criticism, especially in France, for pushing for a stability pact that automatically punishes profligate EMU members and allows for exceptions only in very special circumstances.
On the pact, Kohl said: "I am confident that we will find a solution that will show all citizens the determination of the European Union to create a euro with long-term stability."
EMU should be created "at the planned time and of course, with strict adherence to the convergence criteria," he said.
Kohl also underlined Germany's interest in tightening cooperation in fighting organised crime, having more majority voting and improving the bloc's performance in foreign affairs.

In an aside to critics abroad, the chancellor said Germany, as the biggest member in the EU, was often suspected of wanting a dominant position, especially when it called for structural reforms like changing the weighting of votes in the council.
"We do not seek to exercise hegemonic influence, as some charge," he said. "We don't want to see a Europe where the big countries have the say and the smaller ones are appendages.
Waigel, due to fly to Dublin later on Thursday for a special ECOFIN meeting with EU colleagues to discuss the stability pact, told parliament he would not be swayed from his firm line.
"I will not move away from the clear stability goal," he said. "Every member state must know what the consequences are if it diverges from the stability path.

"The community procedure that then sets in must be transparent and unequivocal... Exceptions because of natural catastrophes or a strong economic downturn that justify going over the three percent limit must be defined as narrowly as possible," he said.
Waigel, who has been criticised in the EU for trying to shut politicial decision-making out of this procedure, avoided the word "automatic" that has irritated his detractors.
Kohl said Germany was still interested in a so-called "flexibility clause" it proposed with France that would allow some EU members to integrate faster than others.
If this was not possible in important areas like fighting crime, he said, willing member states should agree to push ahead by themselves and try to make this EU policy later on.
Greens leader Joschka Fischer criticised Bonn's position as "ritualised stability fetishism" that had more to do with domestic politics than with economic realities in Europe.
He said Bonn's tough line was creating more unemployment in France and putting President Jacques Chirac under such pressure that he could lose his pro-EU majority.
"That is the real message of Nuremberg," he said, referring to a France-German summit held in the German city on Monday.
Both Kohl and Waigel rejected opposition calls for the EU to launch a major jobs programme to fight growing unemployment. This challenge had to be met on the national level, they said.
